extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and tests for determining whether a claimed subject-matter is patentable under the statutory requirement that it be 'new and useful', including what counts as novelty, sufficiency of invention, and the role of utility and results in the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirement: subject must be 'new and useful'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act requires that the subject of every patent should be 'new and useful,' whether it be an art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or an improvement on any of these things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the threshold: the claimed subject must fit into the statutory categories (art, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or an improvement) and be both novel and useful (i.e., capable of being applied to good purposes and not mischievous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent must be for a thing reduced to practice, not an abstract theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent cannot be obtained for a mere philosophical or abstract theory; it can only be for theory reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is an art it must be actually put in practice and unknown before; a mere intellectual discovery unimplemented is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine claims require substantial novelty in structure or mode of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: If it be a machine, it must be substantially new in its structure and mode of operation, and not merely changed in form or in the proportion of its parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor form or proportion changes do not support a patent; the new machine must embody a new mode, method, or application of mechanism that produces a new effect or an old effect in a new way. In complex machinery, focus on what is new in the mode of operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture or composition must be actually made and substantially different
rubrics_metrics.description: If it be a manufacture, or composition of matter, it must be something actually made and substantially different from anything the making of which was before known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claimed manufacture/composition should not be merely a trivial variant of known things; it must be materially different from prior-known articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere change of former proportions or an obvious substitute is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere change of former proportions will not support a patent; the application of what is old to a new purpose is not patentable, and the employment of an obvious substitute is treated as merely a colorable variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: simple proportion changes or substituting steam for hot water where consequences are unimportant are not inventive. If the change would have been obvious or suggests itself readily, it will likely be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of old means to a new purpose is not patentable absent a new instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere purpose, or effect of a machine, however novel, can furnish no ground for a valid patent, unless the machine itself, the instrument by which the purpose is effected, is substantially new. The application of what is old to a new purpose is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protecting an effect without a new apparatus or method is insufficient; you must claim the new mode/instrument producing that effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of labor, thought, or accident irrelevant if result is substantially new
rubrics_metrics.description: Provided the invention is substantially new, it is of no consequence whether a great or small amount of thought, ingenuity, skill, labor, or experiment has been expended, or whether it was discovered by mere accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law looks to the factual novelty and usefulness of the result, not the inventor's process or degree of effort; accidental discoveries can still be patentable if they produce a new, useful result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trivial, frivolous, or colorable variations will not support a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the consequences resulting from the change are unimportant, and the change consists merely in the employment of an obvious substitute, the discovery and application of which could not have involved the exercise of the inventive faculty in any considerable degree, then the change is treated as merely a colorable variation, or a double use, and not a substantive invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations include insignificant substitutions (steam for hot water) or variants that achieve no real improvement; courts will treat these as non-patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and beneficial consequences can establish sufficiency of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The utility of the change, and the consequences resulting therefrom, may be such as to show that the inventive faculty may have been at work; and in such cases, though the change was the result of accident, its utility and importance will afford the requisite test of the amount of invention involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a substitution or change leads to a new, better, or cheaper article (e.g., use of anthracite and hot blast in ironmaking), the resulting public benefit can indicate sufficient invention even if the change was accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material improvement of trade is sufficient to support a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: If there be anything material and new which is an improvement of the trade, that will be sufficient to support a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Improvement of the trade’ means producing the article cheaper or better (or both); courts weigh real commercial or practical improvements when assessing sufficiency of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test: consider the nature of the change and its consequences together
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of invention, and the sufficiency of a change to support a patent, may be estimated from the result; two things have to be considered: the nature of the change and its consequences. When the change and its consequences taken together, and viewed as a sum, are considerable, there must be a sufficiency of invention to support a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four cases arise: (1) both means and result new and considerable, (2) means new/result inconsiderable, (3) means inconsiderable/result considerable, etc. Even minute changes that lead to great utility may be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility in a very great degree may permit presumption of sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever utility is proved to exist in a very great degree, a sufficiency of invention to support a patent must be presumed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptional practical benefits (dramatic cost savings, superior product) can tilt the analysis toward patentability even for modest technical changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Under US law 'useful' excludes only the frivolous or mischievous, not a high utility threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'useful' is not supposed to be used for the purpose of establishing general utility as the test of a sufficiency of invention; it was held that 'useful' was used merely in contradistinction to what is frivolous or mischievous to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus mere capability of use and lack of societal harm satisfy the 'useful' element; sufficiency of invention is assessed separately (see nature and consequence tests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter must be discovered/invented by patentee and 'not known or used by others' before
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a patent must be a 'new' art, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or 'a new improvement' discovered or invented by the patentee, and 'not known or used by others' before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The required 'newness' is substantial: the claimed subject must be something substantially different from prior known or used things; prior public use or knowledge defeats novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess character and purposes of the invention, not the inventor's mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: We must look to the character and purposes of the invention, and not to the actual process by which it was produced, in order to see that the possibility of thought, design, ingenuity, or labor having been exercised is not excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether the product/process could plausibly result from design/skill; if its character makes design impossible, that is evidence against novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: If the alleged invention's character excludes possibility of design, that indicates lack of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the character of the alleged invention be such that no design or study could by possibility have been exercised in its production, then its character is strong proof that it does not differ substantially from what had been produced before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidentiary standard: inventions that could only have arisen accidentally and not by any exercise of skill are suspect as non-novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations of known elements can be patentable if the combination and result are new
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a machine, each part of which was in use before, but in which the combination of different parts is new, and a new result is produced, is good because there is a novelty in the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty can reside in a new combination producing a new result even if components are old; the combination's mode and the new effect are the focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a well-known mode to a single particular case does not necessarily create patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of a mode well known and generally used in several of a class of cases, to one particular case of that class, did not constitute a new manufacture within the meaning of the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: avoiding welding in anchors by methods long used for similar instruments did not make the anchor patentable; courts distinguish genuine inventive application from obvious transposition of known practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a machine does not perform better than prior art, there is no sufficiency of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the gist of the objection was that the alleged new machinery did not serve the purpose of spinning cotton better than the machinery formerly used, the court held that there could not be said to be a sufficiency of invention to support a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical superiority in performing the intended function is evidence of invention; absence of improved performance undermines patentability.
